hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: In a single-server setup, a user types app.example.com into a browser. What turns that name into the server's IP address?
options: The web server, which answers on port 80 for any name
DNS, usually a third-party managed service
The browser's built-in load balancer
A CDN edge node that proxies to the server
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: The browser asks DNS (typically a managed service, not the app server) for the IP, then sends HTTP to that IP. The web server only sees the request after resolution has already happened; a CDN is not part of a minimal single-server setup.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: One server runs the Node app, the PostgreSQL database and Redis. During a traffic spike, page latency jumps even for simple endpoints. What is the most likely cause?
options: DNS resolution slows down under high traffic
Node.js cannot accept more than a few hundred connections
The app, database and cache compete for the same CPU, RAM and disk
Redis forces the database into single-threaded mode
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: With everything on one box, a heavy query or cache memory growth steals CPU, memory and disk I/O from the web process, so unrelated endpoints slow down too. Node can handle many concurrent connections; DNS is resolved and cached client-side.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: What is the main reliability weakness of a single-server architecture?
options: It cannot serve HTTPS traffic
It cannot run a relational database
It requires a CDN to serve images
Any hardware or process failure takes the whole product offline
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: A single server is a single point of failure: a crash, disk failure or reboot means total downtime. It can absolutely serve HTTPS, run a database and serve images itself; those are scaling or performance concerns, not the core reliability issue.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: A Node.js API on an 8-core single server is CPU-bound and top shows one core at 100% while the rest idle. What's the cheapest improvement before buying more servers?
options: Run one Node process per core (cluster module or a process manager)
Raise the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64
Move static files to a CDN
Increase the server's RAM
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: A Node process runs JavaScript on one thread, so a CPU-bound app uses one core. Running several processes (node:cluster, PM2) uses all cores on the same box. A bigger libuv thread pool only helps fs/crypto/dns work, not your JS; more RAM doesn't add CPU.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: You move the single server to a new IP and update the DNS A record (TTL 86400). Hours later some users still hit the old IP. Why?
options: Browsers never re-resolve DNS during a session
DNS changes only take effect after the old server is shut down
Resolvers cache the old record until its TTL expires
The registrar must approve every A-record change
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: Recursive resolvers and OS caches keep the record for up to its TTL (here 24h). Lowering the TTL well before a migration shortens the window. Shutting down the old server just makes those cached users fail; it doesn't speed propagation.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: Why is a single-server deployment still a reasonable choice for a brand-new product with a few hundred users?
options: It provides higher availability than a replicated setup
It is the simplest and cheapest option, and premature distribution adds complexity
It scales horizontally automatically as users grow
It removes the need for backups because data is in one place
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: Early on, simplicity and low cost matter more than fault tolerance; distributing too early adds ops burden without users to justify it. It does not give better availability (it's a SPOF), doesn't scale horizontally on its own, and still needs backups.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: On a single server you deploy a new version by restarting the Node process. Without any extra infrastructure, what user-visible effect is hard to avoid?
options: DNS records must be updated for each deploy
Users must clear their cookies after each deploy
The database schema is reset on restart
A short window of refused or dropped requests while the process restarts
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: With only one instance there is nothing else to route traffic to while it restarts, so in-flight and new requests fail briefly. Zero-downtime deploys need at least a second instance (or socket handoff). DNS, cookies and the schema are unaffected by a process restart.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: In a single-server setup, which of these are single points of failure? Select all that apply.
options: The server's hardware (power supply, motherboard)
The local disk holding the database files
The visitor's browser cache
The one application process serving requests
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: Hardware, the only disk with data, and the only app process can each take the product down. The browser cache is on the client and its failure only affects that user's performance, not the service.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: A user loads a page from a single-server app. Which steps normally happen? Select all that apply.
options: A load balancer picks one of several replicas
The browser resolves the domain via DNS
The browser sends an HTTP(S) request to the returned IP
The server responds with HTML or JSON
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: The flow is DNS lookup, HTTP request to that IP, then an HTML (browser) or JSON (API/mobile) response. There is no load balancer or replica pool in a single-server setup.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: In a typical single-server setup, the DNS service is also hosted on that same application server.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: DNS is almost always a paid or free third-party service (registrar DNS, Route 53, Cloudflare). Hosting it on the app server would add another failure mode with no benefit.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.prompt: Vertical scaling (moving to a bigger machine) only postpones the single-point-of-failure problem of a single server; it doesn't remove it.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:0.explanation: A bigger machine adds capacity but it's still one machine; if it fails the product is down. Removing the SPOF needs redundancy (multiple servers, replicas).

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: What is the main benefit of moving the database off the web server onto its own host?
options: Database queries no longer need a network hop
The web and data tiers can be scaled and tuned independently
The database can no longer become a bottleneck
Web servers can now share session memory
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: Separating tiers lets you size each one for its workload (CPU for web, RAM/disk for the DB) and scale them separately. It actually adds a network hop, and the DB can still bottleneck; sessions are a separate concern.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: After moving PostgreSQL to a separate host in the same data center, one endpoint's latency rose from 20 ms to 120 ms. It runs about 50 sequential queries per request. What's the best fix?
options: Move the database back onto the web server
Add more web servers
Increase PostgreSQL shared_buffers
Reduce round trips by batching or joining the queries
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: Each query now pays a network round trip (~0.5–2 ms), so 50 sequential queries add up. Batching, using a JOIN or IN-list (fixing N+1) cuts round trips. More web servers don't shorten one request; shared_buffers helps disk reads, not network RTT.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Which requirement most strongly suggests a non-relational store over a relational one?
options: Very low-latency access to massive amounts of schemaless key-value data
Multi-row transactions that join orders, payments and inventory
Strong referential integrity enforced with foreign keys
Ad-hoc SQL reporting across many related tables
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: NoSQL stores shine for huge volumes of simple, loosely structured data accessed by key with low latency. Multi-table transactions, foreign keys and ad-hoc joins are exactly where relational databases are the better default.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: After separating tiers, what is the recommended network posture for the database host?
options: Public IP with a strong password
Public IP but on a non-default port
Private subnet, reachable only from app servers on the DB port
Same public subnet as the load balancer for lower latency
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: The DB should never be internet-facing: put it in a private subnet and allow only the app tier's security group on its port. A non-default port or strong password still exposes it to scanning and brute force.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Each web request opens a brand-new TCP + TLS connection to the separate database host and closes it afterwards. What's the standard fix?
options: Use UDP instead of TCP for queries
Use a connection pool that reuses open connections
Open one connection per user at login
Disable TLS between web and database
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: Connection setup (TCP handshake, TLS, DB auth) is expensive; a pool keeps a bounded set of warm connections for reuse. Disabling TLS weakens security and still pays handshakes; per-user connections don't scale.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: You scale to 20 Node instances, each with a pg pool of size 20, against PostgreSQL with max_connections = 100. What happens under load?
options: PostgreSQL queues extra connections until slots free up
Pools automatically shrink to share the 100 slots
Nothing; idle pool connections don't count
New connections are rejected with 'too many clients' errors
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: 20 × 20 = 400 potential connections against a 100 limit; once exceeded PostgreSQL refuses new ones. Pools don't coordinate across processes, and idle connections still occupy slots. Fix with smaller pools or a pooler like PgBouncer.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Why might you give the separated database server a lot of RAM but the web servers more CPU?
options: Databases benefit from caching hot pages in memory; web servers spend time on request handling
Web servers store the database's indexes
RAM is cheaper on database instances
CPU is only used by the database during writes
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: A DB serves reads fastest from its buffer cache, so RAM reduces disk I/O; app servers mostly burn CPU on JSON, templating and business logic. Separation is what makes this per-tier sizing possible.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Which benefits come from separating the web tier and the database tier? Select all that apply.
options: Each tier can be scaled independently
The database can be tuned for its own workload
The database stops being a single point of failure
A crashed web process no longer competes with the DB for resources
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: Independent scaling, per-tier tuning and resource isolation are the gains. With one DB host it is still a single point of failure; that needs replication.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Which new concerns appear once the database lives on its own server? Select all that apply.
options: Network latency on every query
Losing the ability to use SQL
Securing network access and credentials to the DB
Managing connection counts from all app instances
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: You now pay a network round trip per query, must lock down network access and secrets, and must budget connections across instances. SQL works the same over the network.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: Moving the database onto its own dedicated server removes the database as a single point of failure.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: It's still one database host; if it dies, the app can't read or write. Removing that SPOF requires replication with failover.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.prompt: After separating tiers, an N+1 query pattern usually hurts more than it did when the database ran on the same machine.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:1.explanation: On the same host, each query used a local socket with tiny latency. Across the network every extra query adds a round trip, so N+1 patterns multiply latency.

options: Upgrading a server to more CPU and RAM
Adding more servers to a pool that shares the load
Splitting one table's columns into two tables
Moving a server to a larger data center
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds machines behind a load balancer or partitioning scheme. Upgrading one machine is vertical scaling (scale up).

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Which component is usually the hardest to scale horizontally?
options: Stateless HTTP API servers
Static file serving
A single-primary relational database with heavy writes and transactions
A read-through cache of immutable product images
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Writes and cross-row transactions on one primary can't simply be spread across copies; scaling them needs sharding with its own complexity. Stateless servers, static files and immutable caches scale out by just adding nodes.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Why doesn't vertical scaling improve availability?
options: Bigger machines fail more often
It still leaves one machine; if it fails, the service is down
Bigger machines can't run databases
It requires a load balancer that can fail
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Scaling up adds capacity, not redundancy. Availability needs multiple instances so one can fail without an outage.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: You double web servers from 4 to 8, but throughput rises only 30%. CPU on the web servers is now low. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The load balancer only supports 4 targets
Node.js limits throughput per machine
DNS is still pointing at the original 4 servers
A shared downstream resource, such as the database, is the bottleneck
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: When added web capacity sits idle, the limit is something every server depends on, usually the DB, a lock or an external API. Scaling one tier just moves the bottleneck. A real LB handles many targets and DNS points at the LB, not the servers.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: What is a genuine advantage of vertical scaling?
options: Simplicity: usually no code or architecture changes are needed
Unlimited capacity as long as you pay
Built-in failover between machines
Linear cost growth at every size
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Scaling up is attractive because the app doesn't change: no distributed state, no LB. But it has a hardware ceiling, no redundancy, and the largest instances cost disproportionately more.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: A Node service keeps per-user rate-limit counters in process memory (limit 100 req/min). You scale from 1 to 4 instances behind round-robin. What happens?
options: Limits stay at 100/min because round-robin is deterministic
Requests start failing because counters conflict
Users can effectively make up to about 400 requests per minute
The load balancer enforces the limit instead
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Each instance counts independently, so a user spread across 4 instances gets ~4× the intended limit. Shared state like rate limits must live in a shared store (e.g. Redis INCR with expiry) once you scale out.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: At the high end of instance sizes, how does price usually relate to performance?
options: Price scales down per core on bigger machines
Price grows faster than performance, so top-tier machines are poor value
Price is identical per core at every size
Bigger machines are free on most clouds
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: The largest machines carry a premium and eventually hit hardware limits, so many smaller nodes usually give better price-performance and redundancy at scale.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Which are prerequisites for horizontally scaling a web tier? Select all that apply.
options: Servers don't keep per-user state in local memory or disk
Every server keeps its own writable copy of the database
A load balancer or similar mechanism to spread requests
Identical code and config across instances
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Stateless servers, a traffic distributor and identical deployments let any instance serve any request. Per-server writable DB copies would create divergent data, not scale.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Which are drawbacks of horizontal scaling compared with vertical scaling? Select all that apply.
options: More operational complexity (deploys, monitoring many nodes)
A hard upper limit set by the largest available machine
Network partitions between nodes become possible
State and consistency must be coordinated across nodes
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Scale-out brings ops overhead, partial failures and coordination problems. The hard hardware ceiling is the classic drawback of vertical scaling, not horizontal.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Horizontal scaling usually requires the application to be designed for it (e.g. no local state), while vertical scaling usually doesn't.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: A stateful app runs fine on a bigger box, but behind multiple instances its local state breaks. Scaling out demands externalized state; scaling up doesn't.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.prompt: Vertically scaling a single physical database server can always be done with zero downtime.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:2.explanation: Resizing typically means a restart or a migration to new hardware. Avoiding downtime usually needs a replica to fail over to, which is no longer purely vertical scaling.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Web server 2 of 3 crashes behind a load balancer. What normally happens?
options: All traffic fails until server 2 is restarted
Health checks mark it unhealthy and traffic goes to servers 1 and 3
DNS automatically removes server 2's record
The load balancer restarts server 2 itself
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: The LB's health checks detect the failure and stop routing to that target; the others absorb its traffic. Restarting it is the job of an orchestrator or autoscaling group, not the LB, and clients resolve the LB, not individual servers.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Why are web servers often placed in a private network with only the load balancer having a public IP?
options: Private IPs make requests faster
So servers can't be reached directly from the internet, reducing attack surface
Load balancers can't route to public IPs
Private networks remove the need for TLS
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Clients only talk to the LB; backends accept traffic only from it, so they're not directly exposed to scanning or attacks. TLS inside the network is still often used; private IPs aren't inherently faster.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Request durations vary wildly (some 5 ms, some 30 s long-polls). Which balancing algorithm usually spreads load better than round-robin?
options: Random with replacement
IP hash
Least connections
Weighted DNS
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Least connections sends new requests to the server with the fewest active ones, so a server stuck with slow requests gets fewer new ones. Round-robin and random ignore current load; IP hash pins clients regardless of load.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: You need /api/* to go to one server pool and /static/* to another, based on the URL path. What kind of load balancer do you need?
options: Layer 7 (HTTP-aware)
Layer 4 (TCP/UDP)
DNS round-robin
Layer 3 (IP routing)
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Path-based routing requires reading the HTTP request, which only an L7 balancer does. L4 balancers route by IP/port without inspecting the HTTP path; DNS can't see paths at all.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Every instance's readiness check queries the shared database. During a 20-second DB blip, what is the main risk?
options: The database gets more connections and recovers faster
Only write requests fail; reads continue
The load balancer starts sticky sessions
All instances fail the check at once, leaving no healthy targets and causing a full outage
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Deep health checks on a shared dependency fail everywhere simultaneously, so the LB removes every instance, even ones that could serve cached or DB-free requests. Keep liveness/readiness checks shallow or tolerant, and handle dependency failures in the request path.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: How do you stop the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure?
options: Use sticky sessions
Run redundant load balancers (e.g. managed LB or active-passive pair with a floating IP)
Increase the health-check interval
Put the load balancer behind the database
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Managed cloud LBs are internally redundant across zones; self-hosted ones use pairs with failover (keepalived/VRRP). Sticky sessions and health-check tuning don't add LB redundancy.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: What is the main downside of sticky sessions compared with a stateless web tier?
options: They require HTTP/2
They break TLS termination
They make DNS lookups slower
Uneven load, and users lose their session if their server dies
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Pinning users to a server creates hotspots and ties session state to one machine, so a crash or scale-in logs users out. A stateless tier with shared session storage avoids both.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Besides spreading requests, which features does a typical load balancer provide? Select all that apply.
options: TLS termination
Health checking of targets
Automatic database sharding
Connection draining when removing a target
Exactly-once request delivery
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: LBs commonly terminate TLS, check health and drain connections during deploys or scale-in. They don't shard databases, and they can't guarantee exactly-once delivery (clients may retry).

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: During a rolling deploy behind a load balancer, which practices help avoid dropped requests? Select all that apply.
options: Kill all old instances at once, then start the new ones
Deregister the instance and wait for in-flight requests to drain
Handle SIGTERM by stopping new accepts and finishing in-flight work
Fail readiness before shutdown so the LB stops sending traffic
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Draining, graceful SIGTERM handling and failing readiness first let in-flight requests finish while new ones go elsewhere. Killing everything at once guarantees an outage.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: Round-robin load balancing guarantees equal CPU usage across all servers.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: Round-robin equalizes request counts, not cost. Requests differ in CPU and duration, and servers may differ in size, so CPU can be very uneven.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.prompt: If web servers are stateless, the load balancer can send consecutive requests from the same user to different servers without breaking anything.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:3.explanation: With session and user state stored externally, any server can handle any request, which is what makes scaling out and failover simple.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: In a classic single-primary replication setup, where do writes go?
options: To any replica, which forwards them
Only to the primary
To all replicas in parallel by the client
To the replica with the lowest lag
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Only the primary accepts writes; it streams changes to replicas, which serve reads. Clients writing to replicas would create conflicting histories.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: A user updates their display name, the page reloads, and the old name appears; a second later it's correct. Reads go to replicas. What's the best targeted fix?
options: Disable replication
Add more replicas
Route that user's reads to the primary for a short time after their write
Increase the replica's cache size
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: This is replication lag breaking read-your-writes. Reading from the primary (or a replica known to be caught up) right after a user's own write fixes it without sending all reads to the primary. More replicas don't reduce lag.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: With asynchronous replication, the primary crashes and a replica is promoted. What data risk exists?
options: All data on the replica is lost
Writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated may be lost
The promoted replica refuses reads until resynced
Indexes must be rebuilt from scratch
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Async replication acknowledges commits before replicas have them, so the newest writes can vanish on failover. Synchronous replication avoids this at the cost of write latency.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you configure a synchronous standby. What's the main trade-off?
options: Commits wait for the standby, raising write latency and stalling writes if it's unavailable
Reads on the primary become slower than on the standby
The standby can accept writes too
Replication becomes eventually consistent
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: With synchronous_standby_names set and synchronous_commit on, each commit waits for standby confirmation: better durability, slower writes, and writes block if no synchronous standby responds. It doesn't make standbys writable.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: After a failover, the old primary comes back online still believing it's the primary, and both accept writes. What is this called and how is it prevented?
options: Replication lag; prevented by more replicas
Cache stampede; prevented by jittered TTLs
Write skew; prevented by SERIALIZABLE isolation
Split brain; prevented by fencing the old primary and consensus-based leader election
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Two primaries accepting writes is split brain, producing divergent data. Fencing (STONITH, revoking access) and a consensus-based failover manager (e.g. Patroni with etcd) ensure only one primary. Isolation levels act within one node.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: With one primary and one replica, the replica goes offline. What typically happens?
options: Writes stop until it's back
The primary is demoted
Reads are temporarily served by the primary while a new replica is provisioned
The application must switch to a different database engine
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Losing the only replica means the primary takes read traffic too (possibly with reduced capacity) until a replacement syncs. Writes are unaffected because they always went to the primary.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: A user refreshes a comments page twice; the first load shows a new comment and the second doesn't. Reads are load-balanced across replicas with different lag. Which guarantee is violated?
options: Monotonic reads
Atomicity
Durability
Strong isolation
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Monotonic reads means a user never sees data go backwards in time. Hitting a fresher replica then a laggier one breaks it; pinning a user's session to one replica is a common fix.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: Which are benefits of a primary/replica database setup? Select all that apply.
options: Read throughput scales by adding replicas
Write throughput scales linearly with the number of replicas
A replica can be promoted if the primary fails
Replicas in other regions can serve local reads
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Replicas spread reads, enable failover and give regional read locality. Every write still goes through the single primary (and is replayed on each replica), so writes don't scale with replicas.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: Reads normally go to replicas. Which reads should still go to the primary? Select all that apply.
options: Showing a user the record they just created
An internal analytics dashboard refreshed hourly
Checking stock inside the same transaction that decrements it
A public list of blog posts
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: Read-your-writes and reads that drive a write decision need the latest data, so they belong on the primary. Hourly dashboards and public lists tolerate a little lag and are ideal replica traffic.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: Adding read replicas increases the write capacity of a single-primary database.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: All writes still land on one primary, and each replica must apply them too. Scaling writes requires sharding or a different architecture.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL streaming replication, a hot standby can serve read-only queries but cannot accept writes.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:4.explanation: A hot standby replays WAL from the primary and allows read-only queries; writes are rejected until it is promoted.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: Which data is the best candidate for a cache?
options: A bank account balance updated on every transaction
A one-time password valid for a single use
Product catalog details read thousands of times per update
Audit logs written once and rarely read
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: Caching pays off for data read far more often than it changes. Constantly updated balances risk staleness, OTPs are single-use, and rarely read logs gain nothing from caching.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: What's the main trade-off when choosing a cache TTL?
options: Short TTLs use more memory than long TTLs
Too short causes frequent misses and DB load; too long serves stale data
Long TTLs make cache reads slower
TTL only matters for write-through caches
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: TTL balances freshness against hit ratio. Short TTLs reload often (more DB load); long ones keep stale data around. Memory depends on the working set, and read latency doesn't depend on TTL.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: A hot key (homepage feed) expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and query the database at once, which slows down sharply. What's the best mitigation?
options: Lower the TTL so the key refreshes more often
Add another read replica
Switch the cache from Redis to Memcached
Let only one request rebuild the key (lock or single-flight) while others wait or get stale data
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Coalescing rebuilds to one request per key (or serving stale while refreshing) protects the DB. A shorter TTL makes stampedes more frequent; a replica only partly absorbs the burst.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: Redis 7 hits maxmemory with maxmemory-policy set to noeviction. What happens when a client issues a SET that needs more memory?
options: Redis returns an out-of-memory error for that command
Redis evicts the least recently used key
Redis writes the key to disk instead
Redis silently drops the oldest keys with a TTL
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: With noeviction, commands that would grow memory fail with an OOM error, while reads still work. Evicting keys happens only under policies like allkeys-lru or volatile-lru.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: In cache-aside, which write path best limits stale cache entries?

Update the database, then delete the cache key
Update the database, then set the cache to the new value from the request
Only update the cache and sync the DB nightly

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: Why shouldn't important data be stored only in the cache?

Cache reads are slower than database reads
Cache memory can be lost on restart or evicted under pressure
Caches only support integer keys
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: Caches are typically memory-first and evict keys under memory pressure; even with Redis persistence they aren't the system of record. Keep the source of truth in a durable database.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: The whole app relies on one cache server. What's the main risk and mitigation?

Data corruption; disable TTLs
Slower writes; switch to write-behind
If it fails, the DB is flooded; run multiple cache nodes and size the DB for cold starts
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: A single cache node is a SPOF: when it dies, every request falls through to the DB. Replicated or clustered cache nodes and DB headroom (or gradual warm-up) reduce the impact.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: Which techniques help prevent a cache stampede on hot keys? Select all that apply.

Serving the stale value while refreshing in the background
Giving every key exactly the same TTL

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: Which are genuine risks introduced by adding a cache? Select all that apply.

Guaranteed slower reads for hot keys
A cold cache after restart flooding the database
Invalidation bugs that are hard to reproduce
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: Staleness, cold starts and invalidation bugs are the classic caching risks. Hot keys are where a cache is fastest, not slowest.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: With write-through caching, each write updates both the cache and the database as part of the write, so reads right after a write find fresh data in the cache.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.explanation: Write-through keeps the cache in sync on every write at the cost of write latency and caching data that may never be read.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:5.prompt: A high cache hit ratio proves the cache is serving correct, up-to-date data.
options: True
False

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: What does a CDN mainly do for a web app?

Caches content on edge servers close to users
Runs the application's business logic
Balances writes across database shards
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: A CDN serves cached (mostly static) content from edge locations near users, cutting latency and origin load. It doesn't replicate your DB or run your core app logic.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: You deploy new CSS, but many users keep getting the old file from the CDN for hours. What's the most robust long-term practice?

Purge the entire CDN after every deploy
Use content-hashed file names (app.3f9c1a.css) with long cache lifetimes
Serve CSS directly from the origin
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: Fingerprinted names make each version a new URL, so you can cache aggressively and never serve stale assets. Purging works but is slow and blunt; max-age=0 or bypassing the CDN throws away its benefit.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Which Cache-Control directive sets a cache lifetime for shared caches like CDNs, separately from browsers?
options: s-maxage
max-stale
no-transform
must-understand

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: The origin server goes down for 10 minutes. Which setup lets the CDN keep serving users?

Shortening TTLs to 1 second
Disabling compression at the edge

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: After putting the whole site behind a CDN, users report seeing someone else's account page. What's the most likely cause?

DNS TTL is too long
The origin is too slow
Personalized responses were cacheable, so the edge served one user's page to others

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Why might you avoid putting rarely requested assets on a CDN?

Rare files corrupt the CDN cache
You pay for transfer while they rarely get cache hits, so the benefit is small
Rare files make DNS slower
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: CDNs bill by data transfer, and rarely requested files mostly miss the edge cache anyway, so cost outweighs benefit. Serve them from origin or object storage.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Why is URL versioning usually preferred over CDN purge APIs for invalidating static assets?

Purges take time to propagate across edges and can be rate-limited; a new URL is fetched fresh immediately
Versioning reduces the file size
Purge APIs only work for images
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: A new URL is a cache miss everywhere at once, and old pages keep consistent old assets. Purges propagate across many edges with delay and often have limits.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Which are good candidates to serve through a CDN? Select all that apply.
options: Images, JS and CSS bundles
A user's current account balance
Video segments for streaming
Public API responses that are fine to cache for 30 seconds
POST requests that create orders
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: Static assets, media segments and short-lived public responses cache well at the edge. Personal balances and order-creating POSTs must reach the origin every time.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Which are benefits of a CDN? Select all that apply.
options: Lower latency for geographically distant users
Strong consistency for frequently changing data
Less bandwidth and load on the origin
Absorbing traffic spikes and some DDoS traffic at the edge
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: CDNs cut latency, offload origin and absorb spikes. Edge caches are by nature eventually consistent, so they're a poor fit for frequently changing data needing strong consistency.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: On a cache miss, a CDN edge typically fetches the object from the origin, returns it, and caches it according to its cache headers.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.explanation: That's the standard pull-CDN flow: miss, fetch from origin, store with the TTL from Cache-Control (or CDN rules), serve later requests from the edge.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:6.prompt: Setting Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 on index.html is a safe way to speed up a single-page app.
options: True
False

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: What does a stateless web tier mean?
options: Servers never read from a database
Servers don't keep per-user state locally; it lives in a shared store or the client
Servers don't use HTTP cookies
Servers restart after every request
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Stateless servers keep no user-specific data in memory or local disk between requests; session data goes to a shared store (or a signed token). They still use databases and cookies.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: After scaling from 1 to 3 servers, users are randomly logged out. The app uses express-session with the default in-memory store. What's the cause?
options: Cookies are too large for three servers
The session secret differs on each request
Sessions live in one process's memory, so other servers don't recognize the session
The load balancer strips cookies
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: MemoryStore keeps sessions per process. When the LB sends a request to a different server, that session doesn't exist there. Use a shared store like Redis. (The default MemoryStore isn't meant for production anyway.)

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Which is the most common choice for a shared session store in a horizontally scaled web tier?
options: Redis with key expiry
Each server's local SQLite file
The load balancer's memory
Environment variables
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Redis gives fast lookups from any server, and TTLs naturally expire old sessions. Local files and LB memory aren't shared state; env vars aren't per-user storage.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: You switch to stateless JWT sessions with 7-day expiry. A user's laptop is stolen and they want all sessions revoked now. What's the core problem?
options: JWTs can't contain a user id
JWTs require sticky sessions
Revocation is automatic because JWTs are signed
Valid JWTs keep working until expiry unless you add a denylist or short expiry with refresh tokens
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Signature checks don't consult server state, so a stolen token stays valid until exp. Common fixes: short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist/token version check, which reintroduces some state.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: What's the biggest operational benefit of a stateless web tier?
options: No need for a database
Instances can be added or removed freely, enabling autoscaling
Requests never need authentication
Responses can never be cached
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Because no instance holds unique state, autoscaling can add or terminate servers without losing user data. Statelessness doesn't remove databases or auth.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Sessions are in a single Redis instance. It crashes. What happens and what's the right mitigation?
options: Nothing; sessions fall back to cookies automatically
Only writes fail; logins continue
Every user is logged out or requests fail; use replicated Redis with automatic failover
The load balancer recreates sessions from its logs
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: A single session store becomes a new SPOF for the stateless tier. Redis Sentinel or a managed replicated Redis gives failover; apps should also degrade gracefully (e.g. clear error, re-login) rather than crash.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Users upload avatars that are saved to the web server's local disk, then later requests can't find them. What's the stateless fix?

Enable sticky sessions for upload routes
Copy files to every server with a cron job
Store images in the session cookie
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Local disk is per-instance state. Object storage is shared, durable and serves any instance (and pairs well with a CDN). Sticky sessions or rsync jobs are fragile workarounds.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Which of these make a Node.js web server stateful? Select all that apply.
options: A module-level Map of logged-in sessions
Reading configuration from env vars at startup
Saving uploaded files to local disk for later download
Per-process in-memory rate-limit counters
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Sessions, local files and in-memory counters are per-instance state that breaks behind a load balancer. Startup config read identically on every instance isn't per-user state.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Which are valid places to keep session state for a horizontally scaled web tier? Select all that apply.
options: A shared Redis cluster
A signed cookie or token holding the claims
A database sessions table
A global variable in the Node process
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Shared stores (Redis, DB) or client-held signed tokens work with any server. A process global is lost on restart and invisible to other instances.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Sticky sessions are a full substitute for a stateless web tier because sessions survive server crashes.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: With sticky sessions, the session still lives on one server; if it crashes or is scaled in, those users lose their session. Stickiness also skews load.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.prompt: Moving session data to a shared store lets any web server handle any request from the same user.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:7.explanation: Every server looks up the session in the same store, so routing no longer matters, which is the point of a stateless tier.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: With two data centers (US-East and EU-West), how are users usually routed to the nearest one?
options: The database decides on each query
Clients pick a region from a dropdown
Each web server forwards to the other region randomly
GeoDNS or anycast routes them by location

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: EU-West goes completely offline. In a well-designed active-active setup, what should happen?

All traffic is routed to US-East, which needs enough headroom to absorb it
EU users are switched to read-only mode permanently
DNS is updated manually by the on-call engineer the next day
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Healthy regions take over failed-region traffic via health-checked routing, which only works if they have spare capacity or can autoscale quickly. Planning for N+1 regional capacity is part of the design.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: Each region has its own database and changes replicate asynchronously across regions. A region fails suddenly. What's the main data risk?

All data in the surviving region is corrupted
Indexes in the surviving region become invalid
Cross-region replication speeds up and causes duplicates
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Async cross-region replication trades durability for latency: the last few seconds of writes in the failed region may not have reached the survivor. Synchronous cross-region replication avoids it but adds large write latency.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: You fail over by changing DNS, but traffic to the dead region trickles on for a long time. What's the most likely reason?

TLS certificates are region-specific
Resolvers and clients cache the old records until TTL expires (some ignore TTL)
Anycast always prefers the dead region

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: In an active-active multi-region database, the same user profile is edited in both regions within a second. Which approach avoids silent data loss?

Ignore conflicts because they are rare
Retry the write until it succeeds in both regions
Give each user a home region that owns their writes (or use CRDT-style merges)

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: Why is synchronous database replication between continents usually avoided on the write path?

Synchronous replication doesn't work over TLS
It breaks primary keys
Continents use different SQL dialects
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Light in fiber across an ocean plus routing gives ~70–150+ ms RTT, which every synchronous commit pays. Most designs use async cross-region replication and accept a small data-loss window, or keep synchronous replicas within a region.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: What helps keep multiple data centers running the same, correct version of the service?

Automated, identical deployment pipelines for every region
Letting each region choose its own release schedule
Deploying only to the primary region

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: Which are key technical challenges of running in multiple data centers? Select all that apply.

Synchronizing data across regions
Keeping tests and deploys consistent across regions
Eliminating the need for backups
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Traffic redirection, data sync and deployment consistency are the classic multi-DC challenges. Replicas across regions don't replace backups; a bad write or delete replicates everywhere.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: Which practices reduce the blast radius of a regional failure? Select all that apply.

A single global primary database for all writes
Regular failover drills
Avoiding synchronous cross-region calls in the request path
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Independent regions, drills and no cross-region synchronous dependencies keep one region's failure contained. A single global write primary means its region's outage stops writes everywhere.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: In an active-passive multi-region setup, the passive region needs enough capacity, or the ability to scale up fast, to take full traffic on failover.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: A passive region sized too small just fails under the redirected load. It needs provisioned capacity or fast autoscaling, plus warm data.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.prompt: Running in two data centers automatically gives strong consistency between them.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:8.explanation: Most multi-DC setups replicate asynchronously and are eventually consistent. Strong consistency across regions requires synchronous replication or consensus, at a latency cost.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: What is the core reason to put a message queue between a web server and a worker?

To replace the database
To decouple them so the producer doesn't wait and each side scales independently
To guarantee requests are processed in strict global order
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: A queue lets the web tier enqueue work and respond immediately, while workers consume at their own pace and scale separately. It doesn't return results synchronously, replace storage, or guarantee global ordering.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: A photo app enqueues resize jobs. At peak, queue depth climbs steadily for an hour. What's the most appropriate response?

Make the web servers process resizes synchronously
Increase the queue's maximum message size
Scale out workers, ideally autoscaling on queue depth or message age

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Your queue offers at-least-once delivery. A worker sends a welcome email, then crashes before acking. What must the design handle?

The message is lost forever
The queue switches to exactly-once mode
The producer is notified and resends it
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Unacked messages are redelivered, so the same job may run twice (duplicate email). Idempotency keys or dedupe records make repeats harmless. At-least-once avoids loss, not duplicates.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time, and it keeps being redelivered, blocking progress. What's the standard fix?

After N failed attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
Restart the consumer every minute
Delete the whole queue and re-enqueue jobs
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: A dead-letter queue isolates poison messages after a retry limit so other messages flow, and lets you inspect and replay them. Longer timeouts only slow the retry loop.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Events for each user must be processed in order, but you need many consumers in parallel. Which design fits in Kafka?

Random partitioning with a timestamp sort in consumers
Partition by userId so a user's events land in one partition
One topic per user
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Kafka orders messages within a partition. Keying by userId keeps each user's events ordered while different partitions are consumed in parallel. One partition kills parallelism; per-user topics don't scale.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Which metric best signals that consumers are falling behind?

Number of queues defined
Average message size
Age of the oldest unprocessed message (or consumer lag)
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Oldest-message age or consumer lag directly shows how far behind processing is. Producer CPU and message size don't tell you whether consumers are keeping up.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: All workers are down for 10 minutes for a deploy. What happens to new jobs with a durable queue?

They're rejected by the queue
They're processed by the web servers instead
They're lost unless the producer retries
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: A durable queue buffers messages while consumers are unavailable, which is a key benefit of decoupling. Producers keep enqueuing and workers catch up afterwards.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Which are benefits of introducing a message queue? Select all that apply.
options: Absorbing traffic spikes
Returning the worker's result synchronously to the user
Scaling producers and consumers independently
Isolating failures so slow workers don't break the web tier
Automatic exactly-once processing
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Queues buffer spikes, decouple scaling and isolate failures. They make processing asynchronous (no synchronous result), and most give at-least-once, not exactly-once, semantics.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Which practices make at-least-once message processing safe? Select all that apply.

Record processed message or idempotency IDs and skip repeats
Ack only after the work has committed
Use upserts or conditional writes instead of blind inserts
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Dedupe records, ack-after-commit and idempotent writes make redeliveries harmless without losing work. Acking first means a crash mid-work loses the job.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Acking a message before the work is done risks losing that work if the consumer crashes mid-processing.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.explanation: Once acked, the broker deletes or advances past the message, so a crash means it's never retried. That's at-most-once behaviour.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:9.prompt: Publishing to a message queue tells the producer whether the consumer's processing succeeded.

False

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: With 30 web servers, why centralize logs (e.g. into ELK, Loki or a hosted service)?

Because centralized logs are free
So servers can skip writing logs

Database replication lag
Daily active users
p99 request latency

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: A request touches the API, an auth service and a worker. How do you find all log lines for one failing request?

Disable alerting at night
Page on every warning log line instead

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: A developer adds a userId label to a Prometheus request counter. Soon the monitoring system slows and memory explodes. Why?

userId values are too long for the exposition format

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: Average API latency is 80 ms, but some users complain of very slow responses. Which metric should you check?
options: p99 (or p95) latency
Median CPU usage
Total request count
Average response size

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: What is the main benefit of a CI/CD pipeline that runs tests and deploys automatically?

Consistent, repeatable releases with fewer manual mistakes
It makes production immune to bugs
It removes the need for monitoring

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: Which are the four 'golden signals' for monitoring a service? Select all that apply.

Traffic
Lines of code deployed
Errors
Saturation
Number of git commits

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: Which practices make logs useful at scale? Select all that apply.

A correlation ID on every line
Logging full request bodies, including passwords
Consistent log levels so noise can be filtered

False

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.prompt: A canary deployment routes a small share of traffic to the new version and watches metrics before rolling out fully.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:10.explanation: Canaries limit the blast radius of a bad release: if error rate or latency worsens on the canary, you roll back before most users are affected.

options: Copying the full dataset to several read replicas
Splitting data across multiple databases by a shard key, each holding a subset
Splitting a table's columns into separate tables
Compressing a database into smaller files
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Sharding is horizontal partitioning across database instances: each shard has the same schema but different rows. Replicas hold full copies; splitting columns is vertical partitioning.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: A social app shards by user_id. One celebrity's shard is overwhelmed with reads and writes while others idle. What's this problem and a reasonable fix?
options: Replication lag; add synchronous replicas
Split brain; add fencing
A hotspot; give the celebrity a dedicated shard or further split their data
Write skew; use SERIALIZABLE isolation
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: A single very hot key overloads one shard (the celebrity problem). Fixes include dedicated shards, sub-partitioning that key's data, or caching its reads heavily. Replication lag and split brain are unrelated.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: After sharding users and orders by user_id, a report needs to join orders across all users by product. What's the typical approach?
options: Run the join as a normal SQL JOIN; the database handles shards transparently
Disable sharding for reporting queries
Use foreign keys across shards
Scatter-gather across shards, or feed an analytics store or denormalized table for reporting
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Joins across shards aren't native; you query every shard and merge, or replicate data into a warehouse or denormalized view built for that query. Cross-shard foreign keys aren't enforceable.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: A multi-tenant B2B SaaS shards by tenant_id. Most queries are within one tenant. What's the main risk of this choice?
options: A few very large tenants can overload their shard
Queries for one tenant must touch every shard
Tenants can see each other's data by default
IDs can no longer be generated
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: tenant_id keeps each tenant's queries on one shard (great locality), but tenant sizes are skewed, so a giant tenant becomes a hotspot. Mitigate by isolating large tenants on dedicated shards.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: Keys are placed on shards with consistent hashing across N nodes. You add one node. Roughly how many keys move?
options: Almost all of them
About half
About 1/(N+1) of them
None; only new keys go to the new node
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: With consistent hashing the new node takes over only its portion of the ring, about 1/(N+1) of keys. Modulo hashing (key % N) remaps most keys when N changes.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: When is sharding usually the right next step?
options: As soon as the product launches
When write volume or data size exceeds what one primary can handle, after simpler options
Whenever read traffic grows
When you want to avoid creating indexes
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Sharding adds major complexity, so teams first try vertical scaling, indexing, caching and read replicas. It's warranted when writes or data volume outgrow a single primary.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: Each shard uses its own auto-increment primary key. What problem appears, and what's a common fix?
options: IDs collide across shards; use globally unique IDs like Snowflake-style IDs or UUIDv7
Auto-increment stops working past 1M rows; use strings
Shards can't use indexes; use hash keys
IDs leak tenant names; hash them
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Independent sequences produce the same IDs on different shards. Snowflake-style IDs (time + machine + sequence) or UUIDv7 are unique globally and roughly time-ordered, which keeps B-tree inserts efficient.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: Which challenges does sharding introduce? Select all that apply.
options: Resharding data when shards fill up
Hotspots when keys are unevenly accessed
Indexes can no longer be used
Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Resharding, hotspots and cross-shard queries/transactions are the core sharding costs. Each shard is a normal database and uses indexes normally.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: Which are properties of a good shard key? Select all that apply.
options: High cardinality
Spreads load evenly across shards
Matches the most common query pattern
A monotonically increasing timestamp used with range sharding
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Good keys have many distinct values, distribute evenly and keep common queries on one shard. A rising timestamp with range sharding sends every new write to the newest shard.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: Range sharding on created_at sends nearly all new writes to the shard holding the latest range.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: New rows always have the newest timestamps, so they land on one shard, creating a write hotspot while older shards sit idle.

hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.prompt: After sharding, a transaction spanning two shards is as simple and cheap as a single-node ACID transaction.
options: True
False
hld-scale-zero-to-million:11.explanation: Cross-shard atomicity needs two-phase commit, sagas or similar coordination, which add latency and failure modes. That's why shard keys are chosen to keep transactions on one shard.
